messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 65
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Project Manager
  trauma_type: Child's life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 46

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Event Involvement: People who are related to the event, Somatic (Breathlessness): Difficulty breathing or feeling short of breath, Medical Procedures: Undergoing a medical examination or procedure
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma, Mental Distraction: keep mind occupied all the time
  Threat: Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted, Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed, Self-Doubt: I can't trust that I will do the right thing

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Matiu Tevaga, a 65-year-old widowed project manager, spoke about the worst period of his life as beginning in hospital corridors, under fluorescent lights, when his child became critically ill and it was no longer clear whether they would survive. He remembered the sound of hurried footsteps, the clipped voices of medical staff, the repeated movement in and out of examination rooms, and above all his child struggling for breath. What stayed with him most sharply was the sight of their chest working hard for air while adults around them moved quickly, made decisions, and used words he barely understood in the moment. He had experienced those hours as a series of suspended waits: waiting for test results, waiting for a doctor to return, waiting to be told whether the treatment was working. Each delay had felt unbearable, as if time itself meant danger. He could still recall standing beside the bed thinking that if he had acted faster, spoken up sooner, insisted on something different, he might have protected his child better.

In the months that followed, those scenes did not settle into the past for Matiu. Encounters with people connected to that period could unsettle him immediately. If he saw a relative who had been present during the illness, or even someone who reminded him of those days, he felt his body tense before he had fully registered why. Medical settings were particularly difficult. He avoided hospitals whenever he could, would drive a longer route to avoid passing the one where his child had been treated, and postponed his own physical examinations. He described a recent instance when his primary care physician recommended a routine check-up; Matiu agreed on the phone, then canceled the appointment the day before because he could not tolerate the thought of being in an exam room again. Even hearing about someone else’s procedure was enough to leave him unsettled for the rest of the day.

What frightened him just as much were sensations in his own body. Any episode of breathlessness, even mild shortness of breath after climbing stairs or carrying materials at work, could bring him straight back to the hospital. In those moments he was no longer simply winded; he felt a wave of fear and a powerful bodily jolt, his chest tightening as if something terrible were already underway. He became watchful whenever he noticed changes in breathing, and if something in daily life took longer than expected—a family member not answering the phone, a delayed text reply, a meeting running over schedule—his mind moved quickly to the sense that something bad must be happening. He knew other people saw these reactions as excessive, but to him the wait itself felt dangerous.

Matiu tried hard not to think about what happened. He said that if he let his mind go near those memories, everything in him reacted. So he kept himself occupied almost constantly. At work he filled every gap in the day with tasks, checking timelines, revising schedules, answering emails the moment they came in. As a project manager, he could always find one more detail to monitor, one more problem to solve, and he used that structure to keep his mind from drifting. Colleagues knew him as dependable but increasingly rigid about delays; if a contractor was late or a decision was held up, he became visibly distressed and short with people, certain that holdups meant serious trouble. Outside work, he kept the television on, took on errands that did not need doing, and stayed busy late into the evening because quiet gave his thoughts too much room.

Underneath that constant activity was a painful set of conclusions he had drawn about himself. Matiu had come to believe that the crisis happened because of the way he acted, though he struggled to say exactly what he should have done differently. He returned again and again to the idea that he had failed in the most basic duty of a parent: he should have protected his child, and he had not. That belief had spread into the way he saw himself more generally. Faced with decisions, even ordinary ones, he second-guessed himself, wary that his judgment could not be trusted. He often asked others to confirm plans he had already made, then still worried he was getting things wrong.

By the time he sought help, these patterns had narrowed his life considerably. He was avoiding medical contact despite his age and his doctor’s advice, and his family had begun to notice how tense he became when anyone mentioned illness, appointments, or relatives from that period. What finally brought him in was a recent episode of shortness of breath before a routine medical visit he had been trying to force himself to attend; he became so overwhelmed that he turned around in the parking lot and drove home shaking. He said he was tired of living as though another catastrophe were always seconds away. At the same time, he was afraid that talking about what happened would prove what he already believed—that when it mattered most, he had not done the right thing.
